recalled_ingredients.regulatory_basis: adulterant — FDA prescription drug. Illegal in supplements. Found in recalled products.
recalled_ingredients.reason: Meloxicam (Mobic) is a prescription NSAID selective for COX-2, used for arthritis pain. When found undeclared in dietary supplements, users are unknowingly exposed to NSAID risks without medical oversight: GI bleeding, renal impairment, fluid retention, and elevated cardiovascular risk. Users on anticoagulants, aspirin, or ACE inhibitors face compounded risks. FDA has identified meloxicam as a pharmaceutical adulterant in joint and pain-related supplement products. Any supplement containing it is adulterated with a prescription drug.
recalled_ingredients.warning_message: Meloxicam is banned: Meloxicam (Mobic) is a prescription NSAID selective for COX-2, used for arthritis pain.

recalled_ingredients.regulatory_basis: adulterant — FDA prescription drug. Illegal in supplements. Multiple recalls for adulteration.
recalled_ingredients.reason: Metformin is a prescription antidiabetic drug (biguanide class) that lowers blood glucose by reducing hepatic glucose production. When found undeclared in weight-loss supplements, it can cause life-threatening lactic acidosis in users with renal impairment or who consume alcohol regularly. Users are unknowingly receiving a prescription drug requiring renal function monitoring. FDA has identified metformin as an adulterant in weight-loss and blood sugar supplement products. Any supplement containing metformin is adulterated.
recalled_ingredients.warning_message: Metformin is banned: Metformin is a prescription antidiabetic drug (biguanide class) that lowers blood glucose by reducing hepatic glucose production.

recalled_ingredients.regulatory_basis: adulterant — Never approved by FDA. Illegal in supplements.
recalled_ingredients.reason: Rimonabant (Acomplia) was a weight-loss drug that blocked cannabinoid CB1 receptors. It was never FDA-approved — the agency's advisory committee rejected it due to severe psychiatric side effects including depression, anxiety, and suicidal ideation in clinical trials. It was briefly approved in the EU (2006) before being withdrawn in 2008 after post-market safety signals. When found undeclared in supplements, users face psychiatric risks with no informed consent, no psychiatric screening, and no medical supervision.
recalled_ingredients.warning_message: Rimonabant is banned: Rimonabant (Acomplia) was a weight-loss drug that blocked cannabinoid CB1 receptors.

recalled_ingredients.reason: 1,4-Butanediol (1,4-BD) is an industrial solvent that is rapidly metabolized to GHB (gamma hydroxybutyrate, a Schedule I controlled substance / CNS depressant) by the enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase. It has been found in dietary supplements and 'relaxation drinks.' FDA has issued import alerts and enforcement actions. 1,4-BD causes dose-dependent CNS depression, respiratory depression, and death — with a narrow therapeutic window made worse because conversion speed varies by individual. Multiple fatalities have been reported from 1,4-BD products marketed as supplements or 'legal GHB alternatives.'
recalled_ingredients.warning_message: 1,4-Butanediol is banned: 1,4-Butanediol (1,4-BD) is an industrial solvent that is rapidly metabolized to GHB (gamma hydroxybutyrate, a Schedule I controlled substance / CNS depressant) by the enzyme alcohol dehydrogenase.

recalled_ingredients.reason: 7-Hydroxymitragynine (7-HMG) is a kratom alkaloid — and increasingly a semi-synthetic compound — with full mu-opioid receptor agonist potency estimated at 13 times greater than morphine by weight. It is responsible for most of kratom's opioid effects. FDA has cited 7-HMG as a primary driver of kratom's overdose risk. DEA designated synthetic 7-HMG as a Schedule I substance in 2024 under the Substance Use–Disorder Prevention that Promotes Opioid Recovery and Treatment (SUPPORT) Act. Products containing isolated or concentrated 7-HMG carry full opioid overdose risk.

recalled_ingredients.reason: Packaging contaminants that leach from plastic bottles and containers into supplements. Powerful endocrine disruptors linked to reproductive harm, developmental issues, and cancer (DEHP classified IARC Group 2B, possibly carcinogenic, Monograph Vol 101, 2013). 2024-2025 research continues to find widespread contamination in supplements packaged in plastic. Choose glass packaging when possible. Not intentionally added but common contaminant.

recalled_ingredients.regulatory_basis: banned_federal — FDA Import Alert 54-12 (active). Completely banned in dietary supplements.
recalled_ingredients.reason: Aristolochic acids are naturally occurring nephrotoxins and carcinogens in Aristolochia plant species. They cause aristolochic acid nephropathy (AAN) — a rapidly progressive and irreversible kidney disease leading to renal failure. IARC classifies aristolochic acids as Group 1 human carcinogens (upper urinary tract urothelial carcinoma). An epidemic of AAN in Belgium in the 1990s, traced to mislabeled herbal supplements, resulted in over 100 kidney transplants. FDA issued an import alert and advisory against products containing Aristolochia, Asarum, or Bragantia species in 2001.
recalled_ingredients.warning_message: Aristolochic Acid is banned: Aristolochic acids are naturally occurring nephrotoxins and carcinogens in Aristolochia plant species.

recalled_ingredients.regulatory_basis: banned_federal — FDA determined not a dietary ingredient (2015). Subject to enforcement.
recalled_ingredients.reason: BMPEA (β-methylphenylethylamine, 4-amino-2-methylpentane) is a synthetic amphetamine-like compound found by FDA researchers as an undeclared ingredient in supplements labeled as containing 'Acacia rigidula extract' — a species in which BMPEA does not naturally occur. BMPEA has stimulant activity; it raises blood pressure and heart rate and has structural similarity to amphetamines. FDA confirmed its presence in 9 of 21 tested Acacia rigidula supplements (2015). It is not a lawful dietary ingredient. Products containing it are adulterated.

recalled_ingredients.regulatory_basis: banned_federal — FDA revoked authorization July 2, 2024. Effective July 3, 2024. Compliance deadline August 2, 2025.
recalled_ingredients.reason: Brominated vegetable oil (BVO) is a food additive formerly used to stabilize citrus-flavored drinks. In July 2024, FDA revoked its authorization for use as a food ingredient, citing animal studies demonstrating accumulation of bromine in the thyroid and fat tissue and potential for thyroid hormone disruption and reproductive toxicity. BVO is now prohibited in US food. Several major beverage companies had already reformulated before the ban. Any supplement or food product still listing BVO as an ingredient is non-compliant following the effective date of FDA's final rule.
recalled_ingredients.warning_message: Brominated Vegetable Oil is banned: Brominated vegetable oil (BVO) is a food additive formerly used to stabilize citrus-flavored drinks.

recalled_ingredients.reason: Under the FD&C Act's drug exclusion rule, CBD (cannabidiol) cannot lawfully be marketed as a dietary supplement because it was first investigated as a drug (clinical trials pre-dated any supplement marketing) and is now an approved drug ingredient in Epidiolex (approved by FDA in 2018 for epilepsy). FDA has consistently stated that CBD is excluded from the dietary supplement definition under 21 U.S.C. §321(ff)(3)(B). Despite widespread US market presence, CBD supplement products are technically unlawful. FDA has exercised enforcement discretion but this legal status remains unchanged as of 2026.

recalled_ingredients.regulatory_basis: banned_federal — FDA banned internal use (2001). FTC consent orders prohibit marketing for internal use. External use
recalled_ingredients.reason: Comfrey (Symphytum spp.) contains pyrrolizidine alkaloids (PAs) — compounds that are converted in the liver to toxic pyrrole metabolites that alkylate DNA and protein, causing hepatic veno-occlusive disease (Budd-Chiari syndrome), progressive liver failure, and cancer. Germany banned internal comfrey use in 1992. FDA issued a safety bulletin in 2001 and subsequently asked manufacturers to remove internal-use comfrey products from the market. There is no safe intake level for hepatotoxic PAs. External/topical preparations with PA-free extracts are a separate regulatory category.
recalled_ingredients.warning_message: Comfrey (Internal Use) is banned: Comfrey (Symphytum spp.

recalled_ingredients.regulatory_basis: high_risk — FDA Class II recalls (2024-2025). Multiple warning letters to compounding pharmacies. FDA warns agai
recalled_ingredients.reason: Compounded GLP-1 receptor agonist preparations (semaglutide, tirzepatide analogs) have faced FDA safety alerts over sterility, potency, and contamination concerns. Because GLP-1 drugs are administered by injection, any microbial contamination or mislabeling creates immediate serious risk of bloodstream infection, overdose, or anaphylaxis. FDA has warned that compounded versions using salt forms (semaglutide sodium, semaglutide acetate) are not approved alternatives. The growing market for compounded GLP-1s in supplements and online pharmacies without adequate quality oversight represents an active safety crisis.
recalled_ingredients.warning_message: Contaminated GLP-1 Compounds is high_risk: Compounded GLP-1 receptor agonist preparations (semaglutide, tirzepatide analogs) have faced FDA safety alerts over sterility, potency, and contamination concerns.

recalled_ingredients.reason: Delta-8 THC (Δ8-THC) is a psychoactive cannabinoid that occurs in trace amounts naturally in cannabis but is synthesized in commercial quantities from CBD. It produces intoxicating effects similar to delta-9 THC. FDA and DEA have both raised concerns about its legal status: synthetic delta-8 derived from hemp-CBD may constitute a controlled analog of delta-9 THC. Multiple states have explicitly banned it. FDA has received over 2,000 adverse event reports including hallucinations, vomiting, tremors, anxiety, and hospitalizations. Products are often mislabeled and accessible to minors.
recalled_ingredients.warning_message: Delta-8 Tetrahydrocannabinol (Delta-8 THC) is high_risk: Delta-8 THC (Δ8-THC) is a psychoactive cannabinoid that occurs in trace amounts naturally in cannabis but is synthesized in commercial quantities from CBD.

recalled_ingredients.regulatory_basis: banned_federal — FDA banned in dietary supplements (2013), WADA prohibited
recalled_ingredients.reason: DMAA (1,3-dimethylamylamine) is a synthetic aliphatic amine marketed falsely as derived from geranium oil. FDA issued warning letters starting in 2012 and has stated that DMAA is not a lawful dietary ingredient. It has been linked to heart attacks, strokes, deaths (including military personnel), and psychiatric events. Several product recalls were issued. The FTC also acted against companies making false natural-source claims. DMAA is not a dietary ingredient under 21 U.S.C. §321(ff). Products containing it are adulterated and subject to seizure.
recalled_ingredients.warning_message: DMAA is banned: DMAA (1,3-dimethylamylamine) is a synthetic aliphatic amine marketed falsely as derived from geranium oil.

recalled_ingredients.regulatory_basis: not_lawful_as_supplement — FDA warning letters and ingredient advisory listing for DMBA/AMP citrate.
recalled_ingredients.reason: DMBA (1,3-dimethylbutylamine, AMP Citrate) is a synthetic aliphatic amine stimulant marketed as a DMAA replacement after FDA's enforcement actions against DMAA. FDA issued warning letters in 2015 stating DMBA is not a lawful dietary ingredient and that products containing it are adulterated. Like DMAA and DMHA, it is a sympathomimetic amine that raises blood pressure and heart rate with no clinical evidence of safety or efficacy at supplement doses. It is not a dietary ingredient under 21 U.S.C. §321(ff).
recalled_ingredients.warning_message: DMBA is banned: DMBA (1,3-dimethylbutylamine, AMP Citrate) is a synthetic aliphatic amine stimulant marketed as a DMAA replacement after FDA's enforcement actions against DMAA.

recalled_ingredients.regulatory_basis: banned_federal — FDA determined not a dietary ingredient (2019). Not GRAS. Subject to enforcement actions.
recalled_ingredients.reason: DMHA (2-amino-6-methylheptane, also called 2-aminoisoheptane or Octodrine) is a synthetic aliphatic amine with sympathomimetic stimulant effects similar to DMAA. FDA has issued warning letters stating that DMHA is not a lawful dietary ingredient and that products containing it are adulterated. Like DMAA, it raises blood pressure, heart rate, and has been linked to cardiovascular events. It was widely used as a DMAA replacement after FDA's DMAA enforcement actions began. None of the DMAA class analogs are lawful supplement ingredients.
recalled_ingredients.warning_message: DMHA is banned: DMHA (2-amino-6-methylheptane, also called 2-aminoisoheptane or Octodrine) is a synthetic aliphatic amine with sympathomimetic stimulant effects similar to DMAA.

recalled_ingredients.regulatory_basis: banned_federal — FDA banned all dietary supplements containing ephedrine alkaloids (April 12, 2004)
recalled_ingredients.reason: Ephedra (ma huang, Ephedra sinica) alkaloids — primarily ephedrine and pseudoephedrine — are potent sympathomimetics that stimulate the cardiovascular system and central nervous system. Following over 155 deaths, 17,000 adverse event reports, and documented heart attacks and strokes, FDA banned the sale of dietary supplements containing ephedrine alkaloids effective April 12 2004 (21 CFR Part 119). This remains the only full federal ban on a previously marketed dietary supplement ingredient. Sports supplements and weight-loss products drove most of the adverse event burden.
recalled_ingredients.warning_message: Ephedra is banned: Ephedra (ma huang, Ephedra sinica) alkaloids — primarily ephedrine and pseudoephedrine — are potent sympathomimetics that stimulate the cardiovascular system and central nervous system.

recalled_ingredients.regulatory_basis: not_lawful_as_supplement — FDA banned in supplements - not a dietary ingredient (2019). Failed clinical trials.
recalled_ingredients.reason: Fasoracetam is a synthetic racetam-class compound that was investigated as a pharmaceutical for ADHD in adolescents but failed clinical trials and was never approved. Because it was investigated as a drug before any supplement marketing, it is subject to the FD&C Act's drug exclusion rule and cannot lawfully be included in dietary supplements. No NDI notification is on file. It is marketed by supplement companies as a nootropic, but its sale as a supplement is unlawful and its human safety profile is not established for long-term use.
recalled_ingredients.warning_message: Fasoracetam is banned: Fasoracetam is a synthetic racetam-class compound that was investigated as a pharmaceutical for ADHD in adolescents but failed clinical trials and was never approved.

recalled_ingredients.regulatory_basis: banned_federal — FDA banned in 1976 - prohibited in foods, drugs, and cosmetics
recalled_ingredients.reason: FD&C Red No. 2 (Amaranth) was revoked by FDA in January 1976 after studies submitted to the agency raised concerns about carcinogenicity — specifically bladder and mammary tumors in animal studies, though the data were considered inconclusive by some scientists. The EU banned it (prohibited from the approved list). Despite being revoked for over 45 years in the US, Amaranth dye has occasionally been found in imported products. Any US food or supplement product containing FD&C Red No. 2 / Amaranth is non-compliant and subject to regulatory action.

recalled_ingredients.reason: Severe hepatotoxicity. 1 death, 9 liver transplants, 200+ adverse liver events documented. FDA recalled Hydroxycut products (2009). France banned all GC supplements (2025). Australia mandated liver harm warnings (2025).

recalled_ingredients.regulatory_basis: not_lawful_as_supplement — FDA Dietary Supplement Ingredient Advisory List (April 2019). Warning letters to 10+ companies (May 4, 2022).
recalled_ingredients.reason: Higenamine (norcoclaurine) is a beta-2 adrenergic agonist alkaloid found in multiple plants. FDA has stated that higenamine is not a lawful dietary supplement ingredient — it was first investigated as a pharmaceutical drug (cardiac stimulant), making it subject to the FD&C Act's drug exclusion rule. FDA's 2019 guidance named higenamine alongside vinpocetine as unlawfully included in supplements. WADA prohibits it in competition as a beta-2 agonist. At doses used in pre-workout supplements it elevates heart rate and blood pressure; cardiovascular adverse events have been reported.
recalled_ingredients.warning_message: Higenamine is banned: Higenamine (norcoclaurine) is a beta-2 adrenergic agonist alkaloid found in multiple plants.

recalled_ingredients.reason: Ibutamoren (MK-677) is a synthetic ghrelin receptor agonist and growth hormone secretagogue developed by Merck as an investigational drug for growth hormone deficiency, osteoporosis, and obesity — clinical trials were discontinued. It is not FDA-approved, not a dietary ingredient, and no NDI notification is on file. Because it was first investigated as a drug, the FD&C Act's drug exclusion rule applies. Risks at supplement doses include edema, joint pain, insulin resistance, increased appetite, and potential effects on cancer-promoting IGF-1 levels in individuals with pre-existing malignancies.

recalled_ingredients.regulatory_basis: banned_federal — FDA banned synthetic/recombinant IGF-1 in dietary supplements (1997). Only approved as prescription
recalled_ingredients.reason: Synthetic IGF-1 (Insulin-like Growth Factor 1) is an unapproved drug compound — not a dietary ingredient under 21 U.S.C. §321(ff). The only approved form (mecasermin, Increlex) is a prescription injectable biologic for severe primary IGF-1 deficiency. Supplement products claiming to contain 'synthetic IGF-1' or 'injectable IGF-1' are making drug claims about an unapproved compound. At supraphysiological levels, IGF-1 promotes cell proliferation and may accelerate growth of existing tumors. No safe supplement dose has been established.

It is an unapproved research compound with no human clinical trials completed and no dietary ingredient status. recalled_ingredients.regulatory_basis: high_risk — FDA monitoring. Class I recall risk (most serious).
recalled_ingredients.reason: Metal fiber contamination refers to metallic particles or fibers — stainless steel, aluminum, iron — found in supplement products due to manufacturing equipment degradation. Metal fibers can lacerate the gastrointestinal tract, cause GI perforation, and lead to internal bleeding and peritonitis. FDA has issued recalls for products found to contain metal fragments, most commonly traced to broken sifting screens or worn mixing equipment during manufacturing. Detection requires specialized testing; contamination may not be visible to the consumer.
recalled_ingredients.warning_message: Metal Fiber Contamination is high_risk: Metal fiber contamination refers to metallic particles or fibers — stainless steel, aluminum, iron — found in supplement products due to manufacturing equipment degradation.

recalled_ingredients.regulatory_basis: high_risk — FDA announced plans to remove from market (May 14, 2025). Under regulatory review.
recalled_ingredients.reason: Fluoride supplements for children are FDA-regulated drug products requiring prescription — they are not lawful dietary supplements. FDA has not approved any OTC supplement dosage form of fluoride for pediatric use. In 2024, an updated systematic review raised questions about fluoride's neurodevelopmental safety at higher intake levels, prompting HHS to announce a review. This entry flags any supplement product marketing fluoride as a children's dietary supplement outside the FDA Rx drug framework.
recalled_ingredients.warning_message: Fluoride Supplements (Children) is watchlist: Fluoride supplements for children are FDA-regulated drug products requiring prescription — they are not lawful dietary supplements.

recalled_ingredients.regulatory_basis: banned_federal — FDA warnings issued 2019, 2023. Not approved for any use.
recalled_ingredients.reason: Phenibut (β-phenyl-GABA) is a CNS depressant with GABAergic and GHB receptor activity developed in the Soviet Union as an anti-anxiety drug. FDA has not approved it and has not accepted it as a dietary ingredient. In 2019 FDA issued warning letters stating phenibut does not meet the definition of a dietary ingredient. It causes physical dependence and severe withdrawal (anxiety, insomnia, psychosis) even after short-term use at doses found in supplements. Overdose with sedatives or alcohol can be fatal. FTC and FDA have taken multiple enforcement actions against phenibut-containing products.
recalled_ingredients.warning_message: Phenibut is banned: Phenibut (β-phenyl-GABA) is a CNS depressant with GABAergic and GHB receptor activity developed in the Soviet Union as an anti-anxiety drug.

recalled_ingredients.regulatory_basis: banned_federal — FDA determined PHOs not Generally Recognized as Safe (GRAS) on June 16, 2015. Compliance deadline Ju
recalled_ingredients.reason: Partially hydrogenated oils (PHOs) are the primary dietary source of industrially produced trans fatty acids (iTFA). iTFAs raise LDL cholesterol, lower HDL cholesterol, and promote systemic inflammation — mechanisms linked to cardiovascular disease, sudden cardiac death, and stroke. FDA determined in 2015 that PHOs are not Generally Recognized as Safe (GRAS) and mandated their removal from the food supply, with full compliance required by June 18 2018. PHOs are now federally banned as food ingredients in the United States. Any current supplement product listing PHOs as an ingredient is non-compliant.
recalled_ingredients.warning_message: Partially Hydrogenated Oils (PHOs) is banned: Partially hydrogenated oils (PHOs) are the primary dietary source of industrially produced trans fatty acids (iTFA).

recalled_ingredients.regulatory_basis: not_lawful_as_supplement — Status pending review
recalled_ingredients.reason: Picamilon is a synthetic compound formed by combining niacin with GABA, developed in the Soviet Union as a prescription drug for neurological conditions. FDA issued warning letters in 2015 confirming that picamilon does not meet the definition of a dietary ingredient under 21 U.S.C. §321(ff) — it is a synthetic chemical not found in conventional foods and was first investigated as a drug. Products containing it are adulterated. FDA requested manufacturers to stop selling picamilon-containing supplements, and several companies complied after receiving warning letters.
recalled_ingredients.warning_message: Picamilon is banned: Picamilon is a synthetic compound formed by combining niacin with GABA, developed in the Soviet Union as a prescription drug for neurological conditions.

recalled_ingredients.reason: Contains monacolin K (chemically identical to lovastatin, a prescription statin drug). FDA considers RYR with significant monacolin K an unapproved new drug. EFSA 2025: no safe daily intake level for monacolins can be established.
recalled_ingredients.warning_message: Red Yeast Rice (Monacolin K) is banned: Contains monacolin K (chemically identical to lovastatin, a prescription statin drug).

recalled_ingredients.regulatory_basis: not_lawful_as_supplement — FDA banned in supplements (2017). Unapproved drug.
recalled_ingredients.reason: S-23 is a synthetic non-steroidal selective androgen receptor modulator (SARM) developed as an investigational male contraceptive candidate; it suppresses LH, FSH, and sperm production at moderate doses. It is not approved by any regulatory agency, not a dietary ingredient, and carries the same risks as other SARMs (endocrine suppression, hepatotoxicity). No NDI notification is on file. WADA prohibits it. Supplement products containing S-23 are adulterated with an unapproved compound whose contraceptive and androgenic effects are not declared on labels.
recalled_ingredients.warning_message: S-23 is banned: S-23 is a synthetic non-steroidal selective androgen receptor modulator (SARM) developed as an investigational male contraceptive candidate; it suppresses LH, FSH, and sperm production at moderate doses.

recalled_ingredients.regulatory_basis: banned_federal — FDA withdrew approval October 8, 2010. Illegal in dietary supplements.
recalled_ingredients.reason: Sibutramine (Meridia) was an FDA-approved prescription weight-loss drug (serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor) that FDA withdrew from the US market in October 2010 after a large post-market trial (SCOUT study) found a 16% increased risk of non-fatal heart attack and non-fatal stroke in high-cardiovascular-risk patients. Despite withdrawal, sibutramine continues to be found as an undeclared adulterant in weight-loss supplements — one of the most persistent adulterants FDA's Tainted Products database tracks. Its presence in any supplement makes that product adulterated with a withdrawn prescription drug.

recalled_ingredients.regulatory_basis: not_lawful_as_supplement — FDA banned in supplements (2017). Unapproved drug. Research chemical.
recalled_ingredients.reason: SR9009 (Stenabolic) is a synthetic Rev-ErbA agonist developed at The Scripps Research Institute to study circadian rhythm and metabolic regulation. It is an unapproved research compound not intended or approved for human use. Important note: animal studies suggest it has near-zero oral bioavailability, meaning supplement products claiming metabolic or endurance benefits are likely fraudulent in addition to selling an unapproved compound. WADA prohibits it. Supplements containing SR9009 are adulterated.
recalled_ingredients.warning_message: SR9009 is banned: SR9009 (Stenabolic) is a synthetic Rev-ErbA agonist developed at The Scripps Research Institute to study circadian rhythm and metabolic regulation.

recalled_ingredients.regulatory_basis: not_lawful_as_supplement — FDA banned in supplements - not a dietary ingredient (2019). Research chemical only.
recalled_ingredients.reason: Sunifiram (DM-235) is a synthetic pyrrolidone compound and ampakine nootropic — structurally related to racetams but more potent. It has never been investigated in human clinical trials and has no established safety profile in humans. No NDI notification has been filed. It is not a dietary ingredient under 21 U.S.C. §321(ff). recalled_ingredients.regulatory_basis: contaminant_risk — FDA does not approve talc as a food additive. FDA monitors cosmetic talc for asbestos; issued multiple recalls 2019–2024 including Claire's and J&J products.
recalled_ingredients.reason: Talc used in cosmetics and other consumer products can be contaminated with asbestos, a known human carcinogen (IARC Group 1). FDA's 2019 sampling of talc-containing cosmetics found asbestos in 9 of 52 products, triggering public safety alerts and voluntary recalls coordinated with the agency. Separately, IARC has reclassified talc itself as 'probably carcinogenic to humans' (Group 2A, upgraded from 2B) when not containing asbestos, further elevating concern. The primary supplement-relevant hazard is contaminant risk — asbestos and other impurities — rather than pure pharmaceutical-grade talc per se. Many supplement manufacturers do not conduct adequate asbestos-free certificate-of-analysis testing.
recalled_ingredients.warning_message: Talc is high_risk: Talc used in cosmetics and other consumer products can be contaminated with asbestos, a known human carcinogen (IARC Group 1).

recalled_ingredients.reason: Chromium(VI) is an IARC Group 1 human carcinogen (inhalation — lung and nasal cancers).
